issues.legal_issue: A public sector corporation that is an instrumentality of the State is amenable to writ jurisdiction.
material_facts: The corporation was a wholly owned government undertaking, and it conceded that it was an instrumentality of the State for the purposes of Part III of the Constitution.
The employee challenged his removal from service in a writ petition, which the High Court dismissed as not maintainable.
issues.conclusion: The corporation was amenable to writ jurisdiction, and the writ petition was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: An instrumentality of the State is an “other authority” under Article 12 and is amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. The Court also noted that the tests in Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi were satisfied.

predicates.public_sector_employer: The employer operated as a public sector undertaking or comparable public body.
predicates.state_instrumentality: The employer functioned as an instrumentality of the State.
predicates.writ_proceeding: An employee brought a writ proceeding challenging action by the employer.

issues.definition: When an employee challenges a public sector employer's action by writ proceeding and the employer is an instrumentality of the State, the employer is amenable to writ jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may decide the merits of an appeal instead of remitting it when the High Court dismissed the writ petition at the threshold solely for lack of amenability to writ jurisdiction and remittal would prolong litigation affecting the employee’s livelihood.
material_facts: The High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine on the ground that the corporation was not amenable to writ jurisdiction.
The corporation conceded before the Supreme Court that it was an instrumentality of the State.
The dispute concerned the employee’s livelihood, and the Supreme Court considered remittal likely to prolong the litigation.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court proceeded to hear and decide the appeal on its merits rather than remit the matter to the High Court.
issues.legal_principle: Where the threshold objection to writ jurisdiction is resolved and remittal would protract litigation involving a party’s livelihood, the Supreme Court may hear the appeal on the merits. The judgment does not cite an earlier case for this procedural course.

predicates.appeal_from_threshold_writ_dismissal: An appeal arises from a High Court's threshold dismissal of a writ petition for lack of jurisdiction over the respondent.
predicates.respondent_concedes_writ_amenability: The respondent concedes in the appeal that it is amenable to writ jurisdiction.
predicates.remittal_would_prolong_livelihood_disput: Remitting the matter would prolong litigation concerning the appellant's livelihood.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows a threshold writ dismissal, the respondent concedes writ amenability, and remittal would prolong a livelihood dispute, the Supreme Court may decide the appeal on its merits.

issues.legal_issue: Arbitrary executive action may be challenged as a violation of equality without pleading a comparator who received different treatment.
material_facts: The employee alleged that the disciplinary action was arbitrary and violated equality guarantees.
The respondent argued that discrimination could not be considered without identifying another similarly or dissimilarly treated person.
The challenge concerned the employer’s own executive action, including removal for conduct the employee contended did not amount to misconduct under the applicable rules.
issues.conclusion: A comparator was not necessary: arbitrary executive action itself may violate equality and is judicially reviewable under Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 reaches arbitrariness in State executive or administrative action; a comparative showing between two people is not required. The Court relied on E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi, D.S. Nakara v. Union of India, and Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India.

predicates.public_law_challenge: A person brings a public-law challenge to action by a public authority.
predicates.executive_action_challenged: The challenged action is executive or administrative action by that authority.
predicates.action_is_arbitrary: The authority's action is arbitrary rather than governed by a fair and reasoned basis.

issues.definition: When a public-law challenge concerns arbitrary executive action by a public authority, that action is reviewable as a violation of equality without a comparator.

issues.legal_issue: Legislative policy does not shield a law from invalidation to the extent that the enacted law violates a fundamental right.
material_facts: The respondent argued that legislative policy and the degree of reasonableness embodied in it were not judicially reviewable.
The Court distinguished the policy itself from a law giving that policy concrete form and held that the law must comply with fundamental rights.
issues.conclusion: A law cannot be protected from review merely because it embodies legislative policy; it is void to the extent it violates a fundamental right.
issues.legal_principle: Although the wisdom of legislative policy may not itself be open to judicial review, a law implementing that policy must comply with fundamental rights and is void to the extent of any violation, as provided by Article 13.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_enacted_law: A person challenges an enacted law on constitutional grounds.
predicates.law_violates_fundamental_right: The enacted law violates a fundamental right.

issues.definition: When an enacted law challenged on constitutional grounds violates a fundamental right, it is void to the extent of that violation, even if it embodies legislative policy.

issues.legal_issue: Employees of a State instrumentality who are not members of a civil service or holders of civil posts are not governed by Part XIV, but remain protected by the equality guarantees of Part III.
material_facts: The employer was conceded to be an instrumentality of the State.
The employee was employed by the corporation and was not a member of a civil service or holder of a civil post under the Union or a State.
issues.conclusion: The employee was not governed by Part XIV, but the distinction between Part XIV and Part III did not remove the protections of Part III.
issues.legal_principle: Employees of an instrumentality of the State do not thereby become persons governed by Part XIV. The Court relied on Managing Director, Uttar Pradesh Warehousing Corporation v. Vinay Narayan Vajpayee in explaining the significance of constitutional protections for public-sector employees.

predicates.public_corporation_employment: The person is employed by a public corporation that is an instrumentality of the State.
predicates.employee_not_in_civil_service_or_civil_p: The employee is not a member of a civil service and does not hold a civil post under the Union or a State.

issues.definition: When a person employed by a public corporation is not in a civil service or civil post, Part XIV does not govern the employee, but Part III equality protection applies.

issues.legal_issue: Conduct that breaches advance conditions does not constitute disciplinary misconduct unless the conduct falls within a specified category of misconduct or the disciplinary rules expressly make the breach misconduct.
material_facts: The conduct rules separately set out a general expectation of employee behaviour and specified categories of misconduct; the general rule did not state that its breach was itself misconduct.
The penalties rule permitted penalties for misconduct, and the disciplinary rules did not expressly incorporate breach of the house-building and conveyance advance rules as misconduct.

The advance rules provided consequences for non-use or late repayment, including repayment and interest; the employee delayed using or accounting for the advances, and the employer withheld salary to recover an advance and charged interest.
The inquiry officer concluded that the employee had committed misconduct without explaining how the alleged conduct fell within a specified category.
issues.conclusion: The alleged breaches did not constitute misconduct under the disciplinary rules, so a disciplinary penalty could not be imposed on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Where penalties depend on misconduct, the employer must specify misconduct with precision; a general behavioural standard cannot be telescoped into enumerated misconduct, and conduct not specified cannot be treated as misconduct after the event. The Court followed M/s Glaxo Laboratories (I) Ltd. v. Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Meerut. It also held that a breach of advance conditions carrying its own contractual consequences does not invite disciplinary action unless the disciplinary rules specifically make that breach misconduct.

predicates.disciplinary_proceeding: An employer brings a disciplinary proceeding against an employee.
predicates.conduct_rules_separate_general_standard_: The rules state a general behavioural standard separately from specified categories of misconduct.
predicates.alleged_conduct_not_within_enumerated_mi: The employee's alleged conduct does not fall within a specified category of misconduct.
predicates.no_rule_expressly_makes_breach_misconduc: No applicable disciplinary rule expressly makes the relevant breach misconduct.

issues.definition: In a disciplinary proceeding, if the conduct falls outside the specified misconduct categories and no rule expressly makes it misconduct, a penalty for that conduct is unavailable even if it breaches a general standard or advance condition.

issues.legal_issue: An invalid removal from public employment may be remedied by a declaration that the employee continues in service.
material_facts: The employee held public employment with a State instrumentality.

The removal order was held illegal and invalid because the alleged conduct was not misconduct under the applicable disciplinary rules and the disciplinary action was arbitrary and procedurally defective.
issues.conclusion: The employee was declared to continue in service uninterruptedly.
issues.legal_principle: For public employment, a court may declare that an employee continues in service when the termination is invalid. The Court relied on Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagatram Sardar Singh Raghuvanshi and Managing Director, Uttar Pradesh Warehousing Corporation v. Vinay Narayan Vajpayee, and distinguished the general restriction on specific enforcement of personal-service contracts under Section 14 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

predicates.public_employment: The employee holds employment in a public-sector body or other public employer.
predicates.removal_from_service: The employer removes the employee from service.

issues.definition: When a public employee is removed through an invalid order, the employee continues in service.

issues.legal_issue: An inquiry report and disciplinary or appellate order imposing a major penalty must give reasons sufficient to disclose the basis of the findings and the authorities’ consideration of the case.
material_facts: The inquiry officer stated conclusions on the two charges without explaining the reasoning or evidence supporting them, and the report contained inconsistent observations about misconduct and prior punishment.
The disciplinary authority accepted the findings without giving reasons.
The appellate authority confirmed removal without showing that it considered whether the findings were justified or whether the penalty was excessive or inadequate.
issues.conclusion: The inquiry report and the disciplinary and appellate decisions were defective for want of reasons, and the orders of removal and appeal were invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Reasons enable a reviewing court to identify error, expose consideration of extraneous matters, and limit arbitrary or partial exercises of power. Rule 27(19) required findings and reasons in the inquiry report, and Rule 35 required the appellate authority to consider the justification of findings and the adequacy of the penalty. The Court referred to M.P. Industries Ltd. v. Union of India, Vedachala Mudaliar v. State of Madras, and Bhagat Raja v. Union of India.

predicates.disciplinary_proceeding_imposing_major_p: An employer conducts a disciplinary proceeding that results in a major penalty.
predicates.inquiry_report_lacks_reasons: The inquiry report states findings without explaining the reasons for them.
predicates.disciplinary_or_appellate_orders_lack_re: The disciplinary or appellate authority gives no reasons showing its consideration of the findings and penalty.

issues.definition: When a major disciplinary penalty rests on an unexplained inquiry report and orders that do not disclose the authorities’ consideration of the case, the disciplinary decision is invalid for lack of reasons.

issues.legal_issue: An employee should not be subjected to a further punishment for the same alleged default after the employer has already imposed a punitive measure for it.
material_facts: The employer withheld the employee’s entire salary while seeking to recover an advance and its interest.
The inquiry officer observed that the salary stoppage amounted to punishment and that removal would expose the employee to double punishment.
The disciplinary authority nevertheless imposed removal for the alleged advance-related defaults.
issues.conclusion: The employee could not be exposed to a further punishment for the alleged misconduct after the salary had already been stopped as punishment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the inquiry officer’s finding that salary had already been withheld as punishment as a ground invalidating the later removal. The judgment does not cite a separate earlier case for this aspect.

predicates.disciplinary_proceeding: An employer brings a disciplinary proceeding against an employee.
predicates.salary_withheld_as_punishment_for_allege: The employer withholds the employee's salary as a punitive measure for the alleged default.
predicates.further_penalty_imposed_for_same_default: The employer imposes a further penalty for that same alleged default.

issues.definition: When an employer has already withheld salary as punishment for an alleged default, it may not impose a further penalty for the same default.

issues.legal_issue: Back wages following invalid removal from public employment may be reduced for periods of alternative employment and for the employee’s failure to comply fully with the conditions attached to employment benefits.
material_facts: The removal was invalid, and the employee was declared to continue in service.
The employee obtained alternative employment for part of the period following removal and later resigned from it.
For the remaining period, the employee had not fully complied with the conditions governing the advances, although that lapse did not constitute misconduct warranting discipline.
issues.conclusion: The employee was not entitled to salary for the period of alternative employment and was awarded half of the back wages for the remaining period until reinstatement.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinarily, invalid termination entails back wages on the footing that service continued uninterruptedly, but wages are not payable for a period in which the employee procured alternative employment. The Court also reduced the award for the remaining period because the employee’s conduct did not fully comply with the spirit of the advance rules, while recognizing that it did not amount to misconduct. The judgment cites no earlier case for this adjustment.

predicates.public_employment: The employee holds employment in a public-sector body or other public employer.
predicates.removal_is_invalid: The removal from service is held invalid.
predicates.alternative_employment_during_part_of_cl: The employee obtains alternative employment for part of the period for which back wages are claimed.
predicates.employee_failed_to_comply_fully_with_ben: The employee did not fully comply with conditions attached to employment benefits, although the lapse did not constitute disciplinary misconduct.

issues.definition: When an invalidly removed public employee had alternative employment for part of the claim period and did not fully comply with benefit conditions, partial back wages are awarded excluding the alternative-employment period.
